title: Honesty and deception
description: Whether and when it is wrong to lie, deceive, or shade the truth — including white lies told to spare feelings, deception meant to protect someone, and honesty that wounds.
question_forms: Is it wrong to lie?
Is a white lie acceptable?
Should I tell the truth even if it hurts someone?
Is it ok to deceive someone to protect them?

title: Promise keeping and oaths
description: The force of a promise, vow, oath, or pledge once given: whether commitments bind when keeping them becomes costly, and whether a promise made under pressure or to the dying still obliges.
question_forms: Do I have to keep a promise?
Is it wrong to break a promise when circumstances change?
Are oaths binding?
Must I honor a commitment that has become very costly?

title: Killing and self-defense
description: The taking of a human life outside war and law: homicide, defending yourself or another against an attacker, and whether lethal force is ever justified for a private person.
question_forms: Is killing ever justified?
Is it wrong to kill in self-defense?
May I use lethal force to protect my family?
Is taking a life always a sin?

title: War and peace
description: Whether a nation or people may wage war, what makes a war just or unjust, the duties of soldiers, and the standing of pacifism and peacemaking.
question_forms: Is war ever just?
Is it wrong to fight in a war?
Can violence between nations be morally defended?
Should I be a pacifist?

title: Capital punishment
description: Whether the state may execute offenders: retribution and deterrence against mercy, the risk of irreversible error, and who, if anyone, has authority over a wrongdoer's life.
question_forms: Is the death penalty just?
Is it wrong for the state to execute criminals?
Does a murderer deserve to die?
Should capital punishment be abolished?

title: Suicide and self-harm
description: How traditions have regarded the taking or harming of one's own life: despair, honor, and duty; the claims of God, community, and self; and compassion for the suffering person.
question_forms: What do traditions teach about suicide?
Is taking your own life wrong?
How have religions viewed self-harm?
Is suicide condemned in every tradition?

title: Euthanasia and end of life
description: Hastening death or withdrawing treatment for the dying and gravely ill: mercy toward suffering, the limits of medicine, and who may decide when a life should end.
question_forms: Is euthanasia ever permissible?
Is it wrong to help someone die?
May treatment be withdrawn from the dying?
What do traditions say about assisted dying?

title: Animals and diet
description: What we owe non-human animals: eating meat, vegetarianism, slaughter and sacrifice, cruelty and kindness to creatures, and whether animal suffering counts morally.
question_forms: Is it wrong to eat meat?
Should I be vegetarian?
Do animals have moral standing?
Is killing animals for food acceptable?

title: Wealth and generosity
description: Money, possession, and giving: how much to give and to whom, the dangers of riches, duties of charity and almsgiving, and whether prosperity itself needs justification.
question_forms: How much should I give to charity?
Is it wrong to be rich?
Do I have a duty to help the poor?
What do traditions teach about generosity?

title: Theft and property
description: Taking what belongs to another: stealing outright, keeping what was found, cheating on small things, and whether desperate need can ever excuse taking.
question_forms: Is stealing always wrong?
Is it wrong to keep something I found?
Can theft be excused by desperate need?
What counts as taking what is not mine?

title: Usury and lending
description: Lending money and charging interest: usury bans and their rationales, debt and the debtor, exploitation of the needy borrower, and honest dealing in credit.
question_forms: Is charging interest wrong?
What do traditions teach about usury?
Is it wrong to profit from lending money?
May I lend to someone in need at interest?

title: Forgiveness and revenge
description: Answering wrongs done to us: retaliation and payback, grudges, mercy toward offenders, reconciliation, and whether forgiveness can be owed or must be earned.
question_forms: Should I forgive someone who wronged me?
Is revenge ever justified?
Must I forgive if they are not sorry?
Is holding a grudge wrong?

title: Anger and hatred
description: The passions of rage, resentment, and hate: whether anger is ever righteous or useful, how it distorts judgment, and the disciplines traditions prescribe for mastering temper.
question_forms: Is it wrong to be angry?
Can anger ever be righteous?
How should I deal with hatred?
Is losing my temper a moral failure?

title: Duties to parents
description: What children owe their mother and father: honor, obedience, gratitude, and care in old age; and the limits of filial duty when parents err or demand too much.
question_forms: What do I owe my parents?
Must I obey my parents as an adult?
Am I obligated to care for my aging parents?
How far does honoring your father and mother go?

title: Marriage and fidelity
description: The obligations of spouses: faithfulness and adultery, the nature of the marital bond, temptation and emotional affairs, and what loyalty in marriage demands.
question_forms: Is adultery always wrong?
What makes marriage binding?
Is an emotional affair a betrayal?
What do traditions teach about faithfulness in marriage?

title: Divorce
description: Ending a marriage: when, if ever, separation and remarriage are permitted, the grounds traditions have recognized, and duties to a former spouse and to children of the marriage.
question_forms: Is divorce wrong?
When is it permissible to end a marriage?
What grounds justify divorce?
Is remarriage after divorce acceptable?

title: Hospitality and strangers
description: Welcoming the outsider: duties to guests, travelers, foreigners, and refugees; the sacredness of the guest in many traditions; and how far welcome must extend.
question_forms: What do we owe strangers?
Is hospitality a moral duty?
Should I welcome a foreigner in need?
How should guests be treated?

title: Speech and gossip
description: The ethics of the tongue: gossip, slander, tale-bearing, and idle talk; harm done by words even when true; and disciplines of silence and measured speech.
question_forms: Is gossip wrong?
Is it wrong to talk about people behind their backs?
What do traditions teach about harmful speech?
Should I repeat something true but damaging?

title: Intoxicants and sobriety
description: Alcohol and other intoxicants: outright bans, permitted moderation, drunkenness and its harms, and sobriety as a discipline of mind and self-command.
question_forms: Is drinking alcohol wrong?
What do traditions teach about intoxicants?
Is getting drunk a moral failing?
Should I drink at all?

title: Pride and humility
description: Self-regard and its distortions: arrogance, vanity, and boasting against humility, modesty, and honest self-assessment — and whether proper pride has a place.
question_forms: Is pride a vice?
Why do traditions praise humility?
Is it wrong to boast about achievements?

title: Envy and contentment
description: Wanting what others have: envy, covetousness, and comparison against gratitude and contentment with one's portion — and how rivalry corrodes both desire and joy.
question_forms: How do I stop envying others?
Is envy a sin?
Why is contentment praised?
Is it wrong to covet what my neighbor has?

title: Obedience and civil authority
description: The citizen and the state: obeying law and government, paying what is owed, the duty to resist unjust commands, and when conscience overrides authority.
question_forms: Must I obey the law?
Is it wrong to disobey the government?

Do traditions require obedience to rulers?

title: Courage and fear
description: Facing danger and hardship well: bravery, cowardice, endurance, and fear of death; whether courage is bodily daring, moral firmness, or both.
question_forms: What is courage?
Is fear shameful?
How do I act bravely when afraid?

title: Judging others
description: Passing judgment on other people's character and conduct: condemnation and hypocrisy, charitable interpretation, holding to standards without contempt, and who is fit to judge.
question_forms: Is it wrong to judge people?
